blocks.body:
Solving $x^2 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$ is a finite search: try the seven residues and find $x \equiv 3$ or $x \equiv 4$. Solving $x^2 \equiv 2 \pmod{7^{10}}$ by trial would mean checking about 282 million residues. Yet the answer is just as structured: there are again exactly two solutions, and each one can be computed from the solutions modulo $7$ by a few lines of arithmetic.

Hensel's lemma explains why. A root modulo $p$ at which the derivative does not vanish modulo $p$ can be refined, one digit in base $p$ at a time, into a root modulo $p^2, p^3, \dots$, and the refinement is forced at every step. Together with the [[crt|Chinese remainder theorem]], this reduces any polynomial congruence modulo $n$ to congruences modulo the primes dividing $n$.

blocks.title: Lifting a root by hand
blocks.body:
Start with $f(x) = x^2 - 2$ and the root $x_1 = 3$ modulo $7$. Any root modulo $49$ that reduces to $3$ modulo $7$ has the form $3 + 7t$ with $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, 6\}$. Expand:

$$f(3 + 7t) = 9 + 42t + 49t^2 - 2 = 7 + 42t + 49t^2.$$

Modulo $49$ the last term vanishes, so we need $7 + 42t \equiv 0 \pmod{49}$, that is $1 + 6t \equiv 0 \pmod 7$. Since $6$ is invertible modulo $7$ (it is its own inverse), $t \equiv -6 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$, and $x_2 = 10$. Indeed $10^2 = 100 = 2 \cdot 49 + 2$.

Three features of this computation are completely general. First, the square term $49t^2$ dropped out, so the condition on $t$ was linear. Second, the coefficient of $t$ was $7 \cdot f'(3) = 7 \cdot 6$, so solving for $t$ required exactly that $f'(3)$ be invertible modulo $7$ (see [[mod-inverse]]). Third, because $f'(3) \not\equiv 0$, the value of $t$ was unique: exactly one of the seven candidates works.

Repeating the step gives $x_3 = 108$ modulo $343$, and so on forever. This is the same idea as Newton's method $x \mapsto x - f(x)/f'(x)$ for real roots, with "close to a root" meaning "divisible by a high power of $p$".

blocks.title: Hensel's lemma (simple root version)
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients, $p$ a prime and $k \ge 1$. Suppose $f(x_k) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^k}$ and $f'(x_k) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$. Then there is exactly one residue $x_{k+1}$ modulo $p^{k+1}$ with

$$x_{k+1} \equiv x_k \pmod{p^k} \quad\text{and}\quad f(x_{k+1}) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{k+1}},$$

and it is given by

$$x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)\, f'(x_k)^{-1} \pmod{p^{k+1}}.$$

Moreover $f'(x_{k+1}) \equiv f'(x_k) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$, so the step can be repeated. Consequently a root $a$ modulo $p$ with $f'(a) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ determines, for every $k$, exactly one root modulo $p^k$ that is congruent to $a$ modulo $p$.

blocks.title: Proof of Hensel's lemma
blocks.body:
First an algebraic fact. For any integers $a$ and $h$ there is an integer $g$ with

$$f(a + h) = f(a) + h f'(a) + h^2 g.$$

It suffices to check this for $f(x) = x^n$, since both sides are additive in $f$. By the binomial theorem $(a+h)^n = a^n + n a^{n-1} h + \sum_{j \ge 2} \binom{n}{j} a^{n-j} h^j$, and every term of the last sum is an integer multiple of $h^2$.

Now write $f(x_k) = p^k m$ with $m$ an integer, and look for roots of the form $x_k + t p^k$. Taking $h = t p^k$ above,

$$f(x_k + t p^k) = p^k m + t p^k f'(x_k) + t^2 p^{2k} g.$$

Since $k \ge 1$ we have $2k \ge k+1$, so modulo $p^{k+1}$ this is $p^k\bigl(m + t f'(x_k)\bigr)$. It is divisible by $p^{k+1}$ exactly when $m + t f'(x_k) \equiv 0 \pmod p$. Because $f'(x_k)$ is invertible modulo $p$, this linear congruence has exactly one solution $t \equiv -m\, f'(x_k)^{-1} \pmod p$. Different $t$ modulo $p$ give different residues $x_k + tp^k$ modulo $p^{k+1}$, and every residue modulo $p^{k+1}$ that is congruent to $x_k$ modulo $p^k$ has this form, so the lift exists and is unique.

The formula: if $u$ is any integer with $u f'(x_k) \equiv 1 \pmod{p^{k+1}}$, then $f(x_k) u = p^k m u$ and $m u \equiv m f'(x_k)^{-1} \pmod p$, so $x_k - f(x_k) u \equiv x_k + t p^k \pmod{p^{k+1}}$. (In particular an inverse of $f'(x_k)$ modulo $p$ is already enough, since only $mu$ modulo $p$ matters.)

Finally $x_{k+1} \equiv x_k \pmod p$ gives $f'(x_{k+1}) \equiv f'(x_k) \pmod p$, because $f'$ also has integer coefficients. For the last sentence, argue by induction on $k$: a root modulo $p^{k+1}$ congruent to $a$ modulo $p$ is in particular a root modulo $p^k$ congruent to $a$, hence congruent to the unique such root $x_k$ modulo $p^k$, and the uniqueness part above then pins it down modulo $p^{k+1}$.

blocks.title: When the derivative vanishes
blocks.body:
The hypothesis $f'(a) \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ is not decoration. If it fails, the coefficient of $t$ in the proof disappears and the condition becomes $m \equiv 0 \pmod p$, which is either always true or never true. So a singular root either branches into $p$ lifts or has none.

Both happen already for $p = 2$. Take $f(x) = x^2 - 1$, so $f'(x) = 2x \equiv 0 \pmod 2$. Modulo $2$ there is one root, modulo $4$ there are two ($1, 3$), and modulo $2^k$ for $k \ge 3$ there are four ($\pm 1$ and $2^{k-1} \pm 1$). On the other hand $x^2 \equiv 3 \pmod 2$ has the root $1$, but $x^2 \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ has none, since odd squares are $1$ modulo $4$.

For square roots modulo powers of $2$ the full answer is: an odd number $c$ is a square modulo every $2^k$ if and only if $c \equiv 1 \pmod 8$. The necessity comes from $(2j+1)^2 = 4j(j+1) + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$. The sufficiency follows from a stronger form of Hensel's lemma, which allows singular roots provided $f(a)$ is divisible by a high enough power of $p$: if $v_p(f(a)) > 2\,v_p(f'(a))$, then for every $k$ there is a root modulo $p^k$ that is congruent to $a$ modulo $p^{v_p(f(a)) - v_p(f'(a))}$. Here $v_p(m)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $m$ (the [[p-adic-valuation]]). For $f(x) = x^2 - c$ and $a$ odd, $v_2(f'(a)) = 1$, so one needs $8 \mid a^2 - c$, which is exactly $c \equiv 1 \pmod 8$.

blocks.title: Counting roots modulo n
blocks.body:
Let $N_f(n)$ be the number of residues $x$ modulo $n$ with $f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod n$. By the Chinese remainder theorem, $N_f(mn) = N_f(m) N_f(n)$ whenever $\gcd(m,n) = 1$: a root modulo $mn$ is the same thing as a pair of roots modulo $m$ and modulo $n$. So it suffices to count roots modulo prime powers.

Hensel's lemma handles prime powers in the common case. If every root of $f$ modulo $p$ is simple (that is, $f'$ does not vanish there), then $N_f(p^k) = N_f(p)$ for all $k \ge 1$. This always happens when $p$ divides neither the leading coefficient nor the discriminant of $f$, since a common root of $f$ and $f'$ modulo $p$ is exactly what the discriminant detects. For example, $x^2 + 1$ has two simple roots modulo every prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ (the derivative $2x$ is nonzero because $x \not\equiv 0$), so it has exactly two roots modulo every power of such a prime.

The workflow for a polynomial congruence modulo $n$ is therefore: factor $n$, solve modulo each prime, lift with Hensel's lemma (treating singular roots by hand), and glue with the CRT.

blocks.title: Square roots of 2 modulo 343
blocks.solution:
Here $343 = 7^3$ and $f(x) = x^2 - 2$, $f'(x) = 2x$. Modulo $7$ the roots are $3$ and $4$, and $f'(3) = 6$, $f'(4) = 8 \equiv 1$ are both nonzero modulo $7$, so each root lifts uniquely and there are exactly two solutions modulo $343$.

Lift $x_1 = 3$. We computed $x_2 = 10$ above. For the next step, $f(10) = 98 = 49 \cdot 2$, so $m = 2$, and $f'(10) = 20 \equiv 6 \pmod 7$ with inverse $6$. Then $t \equiv -2 \cdot 6 = -12 \equiv 2 \pmod 7$ and

$$x_3 = 10 + 2 \cdot 49 = 108.$$

Check: $108^2 = 11664 = 34 \cdot 343 + 2$.

The other root needs no new work: if $x$ is a root then so is $-x$, and $-108 \equiv 235 \pmod{343}$ reduces to $4$ modulo $7$. So the solutions are $x \equiv 108$ and $x \equiv 235 \pmod{343}$.

blocks.title: A cube root modulo 125
blocks.solution:
Modulo $5$ the cubes are $0, 1, 8 \equiv 3, 27 \equiv 2, 64 \equiv 4$, so the only root is $x \equiv 3$. The derivative is $f'(x) = 3x^2$, and $f'(3) = 27 \equiv 2 \not\equiv 0 \pmod 5$, so there is exactly one solution modulo $125$.

Modulo $25$: $f(3) = 27 - 2 = 25 \equiv 0 \pmod{25}$, so $x_2 = 3$ already (the correction $t$ is $0$; lifts need not change the number).

Modulo $125$: $f(3) = 25 = 25 \cdot 1$, so $m = 1$. The inverse of $f'(3) \equiv 2$ modulo $5$ is $3$, so $t \equiv -1 \cdot 3 \equiv 2 \pmod 5$ and $x_3 = 3 + 2 \cdot 25 = 53$.

Check: $53^3 = 148877 = 1191 \cdot 125 + 2$. The unique solution is $x \equiv 53 \pmod{125}$.

blocks.title: Numbers that end in their own square
blocks.body: The number $376$ has the property that $376^2 = 141376$ ends in $376$. How many residues $x$ modulo $10^k$ satisfy $x^2 \equiv x \pmod{10^k}$, and why do the nontrivial ones always add up to $10^k + 1$?
blocks.solution:
Let $f(x) = x^2 - x = x(x-1)$, with $f'(x) = 2x - 1$. By the CRT, solutions modulo $10^k$ correspond to pairs of solutions modulo $2^k$ and modulo $5^k$.

Modulo $2$ the roots are $0$ and $1$, and $f'(0) = -1$, $f'(1) = 1$ are odd, so both roots are simple. By Hensel's lemma there are exactly two roots modulo $2^k$ for every $k$; since $0$ and $1$ are obviously roots, they are the only ones. The same argument modulo $5$ ($f'(0) = -1$, $f'(1) = 1$, both nonzero modulo $5$) gives exactly the roots $0, 1$ modulo $5^k$.

So there are exactly $2 \cdot 2 = 4$ solutions modulo $10^k$: the pairs $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ give $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, and the mixed pairs give two nontrivial solutions $e$ and $e'$, where

$$e \equiv 1 \pmod{2^k},\ e \equiv 0 \pmod{5^k}, \qquad e' \equiv 0 \pmod{2^k},\ e' \equiv 1 \pmod{5^k}.$$

Then $e + e' \equiv 1$ modulo both $2^k$ and $5^k$, so $e + e' \equiv 1 \pmod{10^k}$. Both lie strictly between $0$ and $10^k$ and are not equal to $1$, so $e + e' = 10^k + 1$.

For $k = 3$: $625 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ and $625 = 5^4 \equiv 0 \pmod{125}$, while $376 = 8 \cdot 47$ and $376 = 3 \cdot 125 + 1$. Indeed $376 + 625 = 1001$. For $k = 6$ the pair is $109376$ and $890625$. The uniqueness in Hensel's lemma is why these digit strings extend consistently to the left: the solution modulo $10^{k+1}$ always reduces to the solution modulo $10^k$ (when $e$ modulo $10^{k+1}$ has a leading zero, as $9376 \to 09376$, the printed number simply looks shorter).

blocks.body:
- Forgetting the derivative condition. A root modulo $p$ with $f'(a) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ may have no lift ($x^2 \equiv 3$ modulo $4$) or several ($x^2 \equiv 1$ modulo $8$ has four roots).
- Assuming the number of roots modulo $p^k$ is always the number modulo $p$. That is true only when all roots modulo $p$ are simple; the prime $2$ and primes dividing the discriminant need separate care.
- Inverting $f'(x_k)$ modulo the wrong number. An inverse modulo $p$ gains one base-$p$ digit per step. Newton-style doubling, from a root modulo $p^k$ to a root modulo $p^{2k}$, needs an inverse modulo $p^k$; with only an inverse modulo $p$, the extra digits are wrong.

Hensel's lemma shows that, for every prime $p$ dividing neither the leading coefficient nor the discriminant of $f$, the congruence $f(x) \equiv 0$ is solvable modulo every power of $p$ as soon as it is solvable modulo $p$. It is used constantly with [[crt]] and [[quadratic-residues]]: for instance, $x^2 \equiv c \pmod{p^k}$ with $p$ odd and $p \nmid c$ is solvable exactly when $c$ is a quadratic residue modulo $p$.

Kurt Hensel introduced the $p$-adic numbers in 1897 precisely to make this lifting into a limit: the compatible roots $3, 10, 108, \dots$ of $x^2 = 2$ define a genuine square root of $2$ in the $7$-adic integers. The [[p-adic-valuation]] is the measure of size in that world, and the stronger form of the lemma above is the statement that Newton's method converges $p$-adically. Closely related lifting arguments appear in the [[lte-zsigmondy|lifting the exponent lemma]] and in the proof that a suitable primitive root modulo $p$ remains a primitive root modulo every $p^k$ (see [[order-primroot]]).

In computer algebra, Hensel lifting is the engine of fast factorisation of integer polynomials (factor modulo a small prime, lift the factorisation to a high power of $p$, then recombine), and of many other computations modulo prime powers, such as extracting square roots modulo $p^k$.

1. Find both solutions of $x^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{125}$, starting from $x \equiv 2 \pmod 5$.
2. Show that $x^2 \equiv 5 \pmod{25}$ has no solution, even though $x^2 \equiv 5 \pmod 5$ does. Which hypothesis of Hensel's lemma fails?
3. Prove that $x^3 \equiv 1 \pmod{7^k}$ has exactly three solutions for every $k \ge 1$.
4. How many solutions does $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{10} \cdot 3^5}$ have?
